q.s: A 42-year-old woman has had progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids for 1 year. She regurgitates undigested food at night and has lost 6 kg. She has never smoked. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that tapers smoothly at the gastroesophageal junction. Esophageal manometry during a wet swallow is shown.
o: Iron deficiency with an esophageal web
Trypanosoma cruzi infection in a resident of the United States
Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
e: Wrong. Pseudoachalasia occurs in older patients with rapid weight loss and irregular narrowing.
Wrong. Eosinophilic esophagitis causes food impaction with rings, not a nonrelaxing LES.
Wrong. Plummer-Vinson causes dysphagia to solids from an upper web.
Wrong. Chagas disease is a secondary cause in endemic areas; no exposure is given.
Correct. Degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus inhibitory neurons (NO and VIP) leaves the LES tight and unable to relax: achalasia.
Wrong. Scleroderma gives a weak, low-pressure LES and reflux.
cl: Dysphagia to both from the start suggests a motility disorder, not an obstruction.
Food sits in a dilated esophagus.
tapers smoothly at the gastroesophageal junction
Lowers concern for cancer causing pseudoachalasia.
q.ch: Dysphagia to solids and liquids + bird's beak + high LES pressure that fails to relax (figure) → achalasia → loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons.
q.tr: Achalasia = "A-chalasia" = absence of relaxation. Scleroderma is the opposite: low LES pressure.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?

q.s: A 49-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a night of heavy drinking followed by repeated forceful vomiting. He has severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to the back. Temperature is 38.4°C, pulse is 122/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg. There is crepitus over the neck and a crunching sound with each heartbeat on auscultation.
e: Wrong. Does not cause subcutaneous emphysema.
Correct. Transmural rupture of the distal esophagus after violent retching causes air in the mediastinum (crepitus, Hamman crunch) and sepsis.
Wrong. Epigastric pain but no crepitus.
Wrong. No link to vomiting and no mediastinitis.
Wrong. A mucosal tear presents with hematemesis, not mediastinitis.
cl: a crunching sound with each heartbeat
q.ch: Retching → transmural distal esophageal rupture → pneumomediastinum (crepitus, crunch) + mediastinitis → Boerhaave.
q.tr: Mallory-Weiss = mucosal tear and bleeding; Boerhaave = Burst, through all layers.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 46-year-old woman has had difficulty swallowing solid food for 6 months. She also feels tired and short of breath on climbing stairs. Her tongue is smooth and red, and her nails are spoon-shaped. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 68 fL. Upper endoscopy shows a thin mucosal membrane in the upper esophagus.
e: Correct. Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron deficiency anemia, esophageal web, glossitis) increases the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
Wrong. Linked to Barrett esophagus in the distal esophagus.
cl: Her tongue is smooth and red
thin mucosal membrane in the upper esophagus
q.ch: Dysphagia + iron deficiency anemia + glossitis + upper esophageal web → Plummer-Vinson → risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
q.tr: Plummer-Vinson triad: Dysphagia, Iron deficiency, Webs ("DIW").
q.q2: This patient is at greatest risk of developing which of the following?

q.s: A 61-year-old man with obesity has had heartburn for 15 years treated intermittently with antacids. Endoscopy shows salmon-colored mucosa extending 5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
o: Intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus
e: Wrong. Not described; dysplasia shows nuclear atypia.
Wrong. Goblet cells indicate intestinal metaplasia.
Correct. Barrett esophagus: chronic acid reflux replaces nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
q.ch: Chronic GERD → squamous epithelium replaced by intestinal columnar epithelium with goblet cells → Barrett esophagus → risk of adenocarcinoma.
q.tr: Barrett: "goblet cells where they don't belong." Distal = adenocarcinoma; upper/middle = squamous.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes this change?

q.s: A 19-year-old man has had two episodes in the past year in which food became stuck in his chest and needed endoscopic removal. He has asthma and seasonal allergies. Omeprazole for 8 weeks did not help. Endoscopy shows stacked circular rings and longitudinal furrows. Biopsy shows more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
e: Correct. Atopic young man with food impaction, rings and furrows, and eosinophil-predominant inflammation.
Wrong. Chest pain with corkscrew esophagus.
Wrong. White pseudomembranes in immunocompromised patients.
Wrong. Did not respond to PPI; rings and furrows suggest another cause.
Wrong. Webs with iron deficiency in women.
cl: food became stuck in his chest
Omeprazole for 8 weeks did not help
stacked circular rings and longitudinal furrows
q.ch: Atopic young man + food impaction + rings/furrows + eosinophils, poor PPI response → eosinophilic esophagitis.
q.tr: "Rings in a wheezer" = eosinophilic esophagitis.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 45-year-old man has recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers despite high-dose omeprazole, and chronic diarrhea. H. pylori testing is negative and he does not use NSAIDs. Fasting serum gastrin is 820 pg/mL while off PPIs. A secretin stimulation test is performed; the results are shown.
e: Correct. A gastrinoma (rise in gastrin after secretin) suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which can be part of MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas).
cl: Ulcers in unusual sites suggest gastrinoma.
q.ch: Refractory, distal ulcers + diarrhea + high gastrin that rises with secretin (figure) → gastrinoma → screen for MEN1.
q.tr: Secretin normally suppresses gastrin; gastrinomas paradoxically rise.
q.q2: Which of the following additional conditions should be screened for in this patient?

q.s: A 55-year-old man with long-standing epigastric pain that improves with meals presents with hematemesis and melena. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg. Endoscopy shows an ulcer with a visible vessel on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb. Biopsy of the gastric antrum shows curved gram-negative rods.
e: Wrong. Bleeds from lesser curvature gastric ulcers.
Wrong. Not adjacent to the duodenal bulb.
Correct. Posterior duodenal ulcers erode into the gastroduodenal artery.
cl: posterior wall of the duodenal bulb
q.ch: H. pylori duodenal ulcer + posterior bulb + major bleeding → gastroduodenal artery.
q.tr: Posterior duodenum → gastroduodenal; lesser curvature stomach → left gastric.
q.q2: Which artery is most likely bleeding?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss. She has an itchy rash of grouped vesicles on her elbows and knees. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL with an MCV of 74 fL. The test results are shown.
e: Correct. Celiac disease increases the risk of EATL and small bowel adenocarcinoma.
cl: an itchy rash of grouped vesicles on her elbows and knees
chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss
q.ch: Malabsorption + iron deficiency + dermatitis herpetiformis + anti-tTG + villous atrophy (table) → celiac disease → risk of EATL.
q.tr: Celiac hits the proximal small bowel (duodenum) → iron and folate deficiency first.
q.q2: Which of the following long-term complications is she at increased risk of?

head: Test
Result
rows: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes

q.s: A 30-year-old man from East Asia has bloating, cramps and watery diarrhea after drinking milk. Stool osmotic gap is 140 mOsm/kg. A hydrogen breath test is performed after an oral lactose load; the results are shown.
o: Fermentation of undigested lactose by colonic bacteria
e: Wrong. Villi are normal in lactose intolerance.
Wrong. The osmotic gap is high.
Wrong. Lactase is a brush border enzyme.
Wrong. An early peak would suggest overgrowth; here the rise is late.
Correct. Lactase deficiency leaves lactose in the gut; colonic bacteria ferment it, producing hydrogen and osmotic diarrhea.
cl: Primary lactase deficiency is common in East Asian populations.
q.ch: Symptoms after milk + high osmotic gap + late breath hydrogen rise (figure) → lactase deficiency → colonic fermentation.
q.tr: Osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting; secretory diarrhea does not.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the rise in breath hydrogen?

q.s: A 56-year-old man has had diarrhea with fatty stools, weight loss and migratory joint pain for 8 months. His wife notes that he has become forgetful. Examination shows generalized lymphadenopathy. Small bowel biopsy shows foamy macrophages in the lamina propria that stain with PAS.
e: Correct. Whipple disease: PAS-positive foamy macrophages; arthralgias, cardiac and neurologic symptoms in older men.
cl: foamy macrophages in the lamina propria that stain with PAS
q.ch: Older man + steatorrhea + arthralgias + neurologic signs + PAS-positive macrophages → Whipple disease → T. whipplei.
q.tr: Whipple: "Foamy Whipped cream in a CAN" (Cardiac, Arthralgias, Neurologic).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

q.s: A 27-year-old woman has had crampy right lower quadrant pain, nonbloody diarrhea and weight loss for 1 year. She now passes stool through her vagina. She smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. Colonoscopy shows patchy linear ulcers with normal mucosa between them in the terminal ileum and right colon.
o: Crypt abscesses limited to the mucosa and submucosa
e: Correct. Crohn disease is transmural (causing fistulas) with noncaseating granulomas and skip lesions.
cl: patchy linear ulcers with normal mucosa between them
q.ch: Terminal ileum + skip lesions + fistula + smoker → Crohn disease → transmural inflammation with noncaseating granulomas.
q.tr: Crohn: "Can't Ruin Our Healthy Nice Granulomas" — think fistulas, strictures and skip lesions.
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on biopsy?

q.s: A 34-year-old man with ulcerative colitis for 8 years has fatigue and pruritus. He has no jaundice. Alkaline phosphatase is 520 U/L with a mildly elevated bilirubin. Magnetic resonance cholangiography shows alternating strictures and dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. p-ANCA is positive.
e: Correct. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with UC and raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma (and gallbladder cancer).
q.ch: UC + cholestasis + beaded intra- and extrahepatic ducts + p-ANCA → PSC → cholangiocarcinoma risk.
q.tr: PSC = Ulcerative colitis man, "beads on a string"; PBC = middle-aged woman, antimitochondrial antibody.
q.q2: This patient's liver disease places him at the highest risk of which malignancy?

q.s: A 2-day-old boy born at term has not passed meconium. He has bilious vomiting and a distended abdomen. He has upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease. Digital rectal examination is followed by an explosive release of stool.
o: Inspissated meconium due to CFTR mutation
Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses
e: Correct. Hirschsprung disease: failed neural crest cell migration, associated with Down syndrome.
cl: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours.
upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease
q.ch: Delayed meconium + Down syndrome + squirt sign → Hirschsprung → aganglionic rectum from failed neural crest migration.
q.tr: Hirschsprung: the empty rectum on exam is the aganglionic segment; the dilated proximal colon is normal.
q.q2: A full-thickness rectal biopsy would most likely show which of the following?

q.s: A 2-year-old boy is brought in after passing a large amount of painless, maroon stool. He is pale. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows uptake in the right lower quadrant.
e: Wrong. Causes urine leaking from the umbilicus.
Correct. Meckel diverticulum: persistence of the vitelline duct with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates and bleeds.
cl: Rule of 2s: age 2, 2 times more common in males.
Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal
Source is in the small bowel.
q.ch: Toddler + painless lower GI bleeding + pertechnetate uptake → Meckel diverticulum → vitelline duct remnant.
q.tr: Rule of 2s: 2% of people, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 tissue types, age 2.
q.q2: Which of the following embryologic structures failed to involute?

q.s: A 14-month-old boy has episodes of severe crying with drawing up of his knees every 20 minutes, followed by lethargy. He recently had a viral illness. He passes stool mixed with blood and mucus. A sausage-shaped mass is felt in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows a "target sign."
e: Wrong. A lead point in adults.
Correct. In young children, lymphoid hyperplasia after a viral infection is the usual lead point for ileocolic intussusception.
Wrong. A possible lead point, but less common in this age group.
cl: stool mixed with blood and mucus
q.ch: Toddler + colicky pain + currant jelly stool + sausage mass + target sign after a viral illness → ileocolic intussusception → Peyer patch lead point.
q.tr: Kids: Peyer patches; adults: tumor.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely lead point in this child?

q.s: A 78-year-old man in a nursing home with chronic constipation and Parkinson disease has a 2-day history of abdominal distension, cramps and no passage of stool or flatus. The abdomen is tympanic. Abdominal x-ray shows a massively dilated loop of colon arising from the left lower quadrant in the shape of a bent inner tube.
e: Wrong. Not typical in this age group.
Wrong. Rises from the right lower quadrant in younger patients.
Correct. Elderly, constipated, neurologic disease; "coffee bean" sign from the left lower quadrant.
cl: no passage of stool or flatus
q.ch: Elderly, constipated, nursing home + obstruction + coffee bean from LLQ → sigmoid volvulus.
q.tr: Sigmoid volvulus in the elderly; midgut volvulus in infants; cecal in young adults.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant 2 weeks ago has had sudden severe periumbilical pain for 4 hours. Examination shows a soft abdomen with mild tenderness. Serum lactate is 6.2 mmol/L and her white blood cell count is 19,000/mm³.
o: Embolus to the superior mesenteric artery
Ischemic colitis of the splenic flexure
e: Correct. Acute mesenteric ischemia: AF embolus to the SMA causes pain out of proportion to exam with lactic acidosis.
Wrong. Peritonitis with a rigid abdomen.
Wrong. Milder pain with bloody diarrhea.
cl: atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant
Pain out of proportion to findings.
q.ch: AF off anticoagulation + sudden severe pain + benign exam + high lactate → SMA embolus → acute mesenteric ischemia.
q.tr: "Pain out of proportion to physical exam" = mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 74-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of painless bright red blood per rectum. He has exertional syncope. Examination shows a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL. Colonoscopy shows small, flat, cherry-red vascular lesions in the cecum.
o: Angiodysplasia associated with acquired von Willebrand deficiency
e: Correct. Heyde syndrome: aortic stenosis with angiodysplasia; high shear stress degrades vWF multimers.
cl: painless bright red blood per rectum
cherry-red vascular lesions in the cecum
Angiodysplasia, most often in the cecum and right colon.
q.ch: Elderly + aortic stenosis + painless bleeding from cecal vascular lesions → angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome).
q.tr: Aortic stenosis + GI bleeding = Heyde syndrome.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the bleeding?

q.s: A 17-year-old girl has rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy shows more than 200 adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Her family pedigree is shown; the arrow marks the patient.
o: Mutation of the APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q
e: Wrong. A step in sporadic carcinogenesis.
Correct. Familial adenomatous polyposis: autosomal dominant, hundreds to thousands of polyps, 100% progression to cancer without colectomy.
Wrong. Lynch syndrome causes few polyps.
Wrong. Autosomal recessive; would not appear in every generation.
q.ch: Hundreds of adenomas in a teenager + affected in every generation (figure) → FAP → APC on 5q → prophylactic colectomy.
q.tr: FAP: "5 letters in polyp → chromosome 5"; Lynch: few polyps, right-sided, mismatch repair.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely genetic defect?
q.fc: Family pedigree (shaded = colon polyposis or colon cancer)

q.s: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Colonoscopy shows only one other polyp. His father had colon cancer at 48 and his paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at 50. Tumor histology shows microsatellite instability.
e: Correct. Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): autosomal dominant mismatch repair defect with microsatellite instability, right-sided colon cancer and endometrial and ovarian cancers.
q.ch: Early, right-sided colon cancer + few polyps + family endometrial cancer + MSI → Lynch → mismatch repair defect.
q.tr: Lynch "3-2-1" rule: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 under 50.
q.q2: Which of the following processes is most likely defective?

q.s: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain. Examination shows dark brown macules on his lips, buccal mucosa and fingers. Endoscopy shows multiple polyps in the jejunum; biopsy shows branching smooth muscle with normal-appearing mucosa.
e: Correct. Peutz-Jeghers: autosomal dominant (STK11), hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation, increased risk of breast, colorectal, gastric, small bowel and pancreatic cancers.
cl: dark brown macules on his lips, buccal mucosa and fingers
recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain
q.ch: Mucocutaneous pigmentation + hamartomatous small bowel polyps → Peutz-Jeghers → cancer risk.
q.tr: Peutz-Jeghers: freckles on the lips + hamartomas in the gut.
q.q2: Which of the following is this patient at increased risk for?

q.s: A 50-year-old man has fatigue, joint pain in his second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and erectile dysfunction. His skin is bronze. Glucose is 210 mg/dL. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated. His iron studies are shown.
e: Correct. Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE, C282Y) causes iron deposition, cirrhosis and HCC; also restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
q.ch: Bronze skin + diabetes + MCP arthropathy + hypogonadism + very high transferrin saturation and ferritin, low TIBC (table) → hemochromatosis → cirrhosis/HCC.
q.tr: Hemochromatosis: high ferritin, high iron, high saturation, LOW TIBC.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of death if this condition is untreated?

q.s: A 17-year-old boy has a tremor, slurred speech and declining school performance. He has become irritable. Examination shows a golden-brown ring at the edge of the cornea. ALT is 120 U/L. Serum ceruloplasmin is low and 24-hour urine copper is high.
e: Wrong. HFE is recessive and causes hemochromatosis.
Correct. Wilson disease: defective hepatocyte copper transporter impairs biliary excretion and incorporation into ceruloplasmin.
cl: golden-brown ring at the edge of the cornea
q.ch: Young patient + liver injury + movement disorder + KF ring + low ceruloplasmin + high urine copper → Wilson disease → ATP7B, recessive.
q.tr: Wilson = ATP7B on chromosome 13 — "Wilson's Copper Trouble (7B)."
q.q2: Which of the following is the inheritance and defective gene?

q.s: A 48-year-old woman has severe itching and fatigue for 1 year. She also has dry eyes and dry mouth. Examination shows xanthelasmas. Alkaline phosphatase is 610 U/L. Ultrasound shows a normal extrahepatic biliary tree. Antimitochondrial antibodies are positive.
o: Lymphocytic infiltration and granulomatous destruction of intralobular bile ducts
Concentric "onion skin" fibrosis of extrahepatic ducts
q.ch: Middle-aged woman + pruritus + cholestasis + normal extrahepatic ducts + AMA → PBC → granulomatous destruction of intralobular ducts.
q.tr: PBC: "Primary Biliary = Small ducts; AMA; woman." Treat with ursodiol.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely pathologic finding?

q.s: A 32-year-old woman with polycythemia vera has had abdominal pain and swelling for 3 weeks. The liver is enlarged and tender, and there is shifting dullness. There is no jugular venous distension. Doppler ultrasound shows absent flow in the hepatic veins.
o: Bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules only
e: Correct. Budd-Chiari syndrome: hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes centrilobular congestion ("nutmeg liver").
cl: absent flow in the hepatic veins
q.ch: Hypercoagulable state + painful hepatomegaly + ascites + no JVD + hepatic vein occlusion → Budd-Chiari → centrilobular congestion.
q.tr: Nutmeg liver without JVD = Budd-Chiari; with JVD = right heart failure.
q.q2: Which of the following would most likely be seen on liver biopsy?

q.s: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 16 hours after taking an unknown number of tablets in a suicide attempt. She has nausea and right upper quadrant tenderness. Her test results are shown.
o: Chelates the drug in the gut
Binds Fab fragments to the drug
e: Wrong. Activated charcoal adsorbs drugs but is too late at 16 hours.
Correct. Acetaminophen overdose: NAPQI depletes glutathione and causes centrilobular necrosis; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.
cl: 16 hours after taking an unknown number of tablets
Time to plot on the nomogram.
q.ch: Overdose + level above the treatment line + transaminases in the thousands + high INR (table) → acetaminophen toxicity → N-acetylcysteine.
q.tr: Acetaminophen → NAPQI → needs glutathione → NAC gives "N-A-C = Not A Corpse."
q.q2: Which of the following is the mechanism of the antidote that should be given?

q.s: A 7-year-old boy has repeated vomiting and becomes confused 5 days after recovering from chickenpox. His mother gave him a pain reliever for his fever. He develops seizures. Serum ammonia and liver enzymes are elevated; glucose is 48 mg/dL.
e: Correct. Reye syndrome: aspirin in children with viral illness (VZV, influenza) causes mitochondrial injury, microvesicular steatosis and encephalopathy.
Wrong. Safe for fever in children.
cl: a pain reliever for his fever
Serum ammonia and liver enzymes are elevated
q.ch: Child + recent VZV + aspirin + vomiting, encephalopathy, high ammonia, hypoglycemia → Reye syndrome.
q.tr: Aspirin is avoided in children except for Kawasaki disease.
q.q2: Which drug did he most likely receive?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis becomes confused and sleepy 2 days after an episode of upper GI bleeding. Examination shows flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. There is no focal deficit. Head CT is normal.
e: Correct. Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria to acids that trap ammonia as NH4+; rifaximin is added for recurrence.
cl: after an episode of upper GI bleeding
Blood in the gut is a protein load.
q.ch: Cirrhosis + GI bleed (protein load) + confusion + asterixis → hepatic encephalopathy → lactulose.
q.tr: Ammonia goes up with GI bleeds, infection, constipation, diuretics, sedatives.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

q.s: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis from hepatitis C has increasing abdominal girth, fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. She is confused. Diagnostic paracentesis results are shown.
e: Correct. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is usually caused by gram-negative organisms such as E. coli and Klebsiella; ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ confirm it.
Wrong. Polymicrobial anaerobes suggest secondary peritonitis.
q.ch: Cirrhotic ascites + fever + SAAG 1.8 (portal hypertension) + PMN ≥250 + gram-negative rods (table) → SBP → E. coli.
q.tr: SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension; ascitic PMN ≥250 = SBP.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely organism?

q.s: Two brothers aged 20 and 24 are evaluated for jaundice. Both are otherwise well with normal liver enzymes, normal complete blood counts and no hemolysis. Brother 2 has noticed dark urine. Their test results are shown.
o: Defective hepatocyte excretion of conjugated bilirubin
Obstruction of the common bile duct
e: Wrong. Rotor syndrome has no black liver.
Wrong. Crigler-Najjar type I; severe in infancy.
Correct. Dubin-Johnson syndrome: conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from defective canalicular excretion (MRP2), with a black liver.
Wrong. Enzymes would be cholestatic and abnormal.
cl: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in urine.
q.ch: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + urine bilirubin + normal enzymes + black liver (table) → Dubin-Johnson → defective excretion.
q.tr: Dubin-Johnson = Dark liver; Rotor = Regular liver.
q.q2: What is the most likely defect in Brother 2?

q.s: A 3-day-old boy has severe jaundice that has worsened despite phototherapy. Total bilirubin is 28 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated. There is no hemolysis. He develops lethargy, poor feeding and arching of the back.
e: Wrong. Not this severe or refractory.
Correct. Crigler-Najjar type I presents early with very high unconjugated bilirubin and kernicterus.
q.ch: Neonate + very high unconjugated bilirubin + no hemolysis + kernicterus → Crigler-Najjar type I → absent UGT.
q.tr: Type II responds to phenobarbital; type I does not.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 5-week-old girl has jaundice that began at 2 weeks of age. She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her stools are pale and her urine is dark. Total bilirubin is 7.8 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 5.9 mg/dL. GGT is markedly elevated. Ultrasound shows an absent gallbladder.
e: Wrong. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated.
Wrong. Not useful in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Correct. Biliary atresia: fibro-obliterative destruction of extrahepatic bile ducts; early Kasai procedure, with liver transplant if it fails.
cl: Her stools are pale and her urine is dark
q.ch: Infant + persistent conjugated jaundice + acholic stools + high GGT + absent gallbladder → biliary atresia → Kasai.
q.tr: Biliary atresia is the most common reason for pediatric liver transplantation.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 68-year-old woman has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. She becomes confused and her blood pressure falls to 84/50 mmHg. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct.
e: Correct. Acute cholangitis with Reynolds pentad needs urgent decompression.
cl: fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
She becomes confused and her blood pressure falls
q.ch: Charcot triad + confusion + hypotension (Reynolds) + dilated CBD → ascending cholangitis → urgent ERCP.
q.tr: Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain. Add shock and confusion = Reynolds pentad.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment after resuscitation and antibiotics?

q.s: An 80-year-old woman has had vomiting and abdominal distension for 3 days. She has a history of recurrent biliary colic. Abdominal x-ray shows dilated small bowel loops and air in the biliary tree. A rounded opacity is seen in the right lower quadrant.
e: Wrong. Gas in the gallbladder wall without obstruction.
Correct. Fistula between the gallbladder and the GI tract lets a stone enter and obstruct, often at the ileocecal valve; air in the biliary tree.
cl: Stone impacted at the ileocecal valve.
q.ch: Elderly + gallstones + small bowel obstruction + pneumobilia + RLQ stone → gallstone ileus.
q.tr: Rigler triad: small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 36-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back for 12 hours. He does not drink alcohol and has no gallstones on ultrasound. He has eruptive xanthomas on his buttocks. His test results are shown.
e: Correct. Triglycerides >1000 mg/dL cause acute pancreatitis.
cl: epigastric pain radiating to the back
Excludes the second most common cause.
q.ch: Epigastric pain to the back + lipase >3× normal + TG 2,400 (table) + eruptive xanthomas → hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis.
q.tr: GET SMASHED: Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcemia/Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute condition?

q.s: A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has weight loss, dark urine, pale stools and itching. Examination shows jaundice and a nontender, palpable gallbladder. He had redness and tenderness in his left calf last month, followed by similar findings in his right arm. CA 19-9 is elevated.
e: Wrong. Not with a palpable gallbladder.
Correct. Painless jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and elevated CA 19-9.
cl: redness and tenderness in his left calf last month, followed by similar findings in his right arm
q.ch: Older smoker + painless obstructive jaundice + Courvoisier sign + migratory thrombophlebitis + CA 19-9 → pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.
q.tr: Courvoisier: a palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be stones.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has worsening shortness of breath. Chest CT shows panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes. He also has elevated liver enzymes and mild hepatomegaly. Liver biopsy shows periodic acid-Schiff–positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes.
o: Accumulation of misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum
e: Correct. α1-antitrypsin deficiency: misfolded protein aggregates in hepatocytes cause cirrhosis; lack of circulating enzyme inhibitor causes panacinar emphysema.
cl: Emphysema in a nonsmoker points to an inherited cause.
panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes
elevated liver enzymes and mild hepatomegaly
q.ch: Young nonsmoker + lower-lobe panacinar emphysema + liver disease + PAS-positive globules → α1-antitrypsin deficiency → misfolded protein in hepatocyte ER.
q.tr: Lungs suffer from too little enzyme inhibitor; the liver suffers from too much retained protein.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the liver findings?

q.s: A 58-year-old man from a region where hepatitis B is common has cirrhosis. He has new right upper quadrant pain, weight loss and worsening ascites. Serum α-fetoprotein is 1,850 ng/mL. CT shows a liver mass with arterial-phase enhancement and washout on delayed images.
o: Peritoneal seeding before any liver growth
Invasion of the portal and hepatic veins
Early lymphatic spread to supraclavicular nodes
e: Wrong. AFP and imaging indicate malignancy.
Correct. Hepatocellular carcinoma spreads hematogenously and invades the portal or hepatic veins, which can cause Budd-Chiari syndrome.
q.ch: HBV cirrhosis + rising AFP + arterial-enhancing mass with washout → HCC → vascular invasion.
q.tr: HCC: diagnose by imaging plus AFP in cirrhosis; biopsy often not needed.
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to occur as this tumor spreads?

q.s: A 70-year-old woman has left lower quadrant pain, fever and constipation for 2 days. She eats a low-fiber diet. Temperature is 38.5°C and there is tenderness in the left lower quadrant. White blood cell count is 15,800/mm³. CT shows fat stranding around the sigmoid colon with multiple outpouchings.
o: CT of the abdomen with contrast
e: Correct. Diverticulitis: colonoscopy is avoided acutely because of perforation risk; it is done after recovery to exclude cancer.
cl: fat stranding around the sigmoid colon
q.ch: Elderly + LLQ pain + fever + leukocytosis + sigmoid diverticula with stranding → diverticulitis → avoid colonoscopy acutely.
q.tr: Diverticulosis bleeds painlessly; diverticulitis hurts and causes fever.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to avoid during the acute episode?

q.s: A 4-week-old firstborn boy has projectile, nonbilious vomiting after every feed for 1 week. He seems hungry immediately after vomiting. An olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. His mother was given erythromycin for a chest infection when he was 1 week old.
e: Correct. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: loss of gastric HCl causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia.
cl: Macrolide exposure is a risk factor.
q.ch: Infant aged 2–6 weeks + projectile nonbilious vomiting + olive mass → pyloric stenosis → hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
q.tr: Vomiting = loss of acid = alkalosis; diarrhea = loss of base = acidosis.
q.q2: Which of the following acid-base and electrolyte findings is most likely?
